title: Skillful means (Kern ch. 2)
hookLine: the Buddhas teach in many ways, fitted to their hearers, toward one goal

lines: THE DOOR THIS KID CAN USE.
cards: A kid at a kitchen table is stuck on fractions. Her aunt tries the textbook way. Blank look.
She cuts an orange into pieces. Still nothing. Then she says: you and your friends split a pizza.
And the face changes. Same fraction, third way of saying it. Nobody would call the aunt a liar for using pizza.
She found the door this kid could walk through. The Lotus Sutra's second chapter is about that kind of teacher, on a very large scale.

teach.b: In chapter two the Buddha rises from his meditation and speaks, not to the crowd at large, but to Sariputra, the disciple known for wisdom.
The knowledge of the Buddhas, he says, is deep and hard to understand, and then he says he will stop there. Sariputra asks him to go on. He declines.

Sariputra asks again, then a third time, and only then does the Buddha agree. In Kern's translation, as he begins, a group in the assembly gets up and leaves, sure they've already understood. The Buddha lets them go.
Not everyone is ready to hear everything at once, and he doesn't force it. The chapter's Sanskrit name is built on upaya, usually translated skillful means, or skill in means.
The Buddhas teach in many ways: stories, comparisons, reasons, examples, each fitted to the people in front of them, because hearers differ in what they want and what they can take in.
Here is the turn that makes the Lotus the Lotus. The many ways are not many destinations.
The Buddhas appear in the world for one great purpose: to open the Buddha-knowledge to beings, show it to them, and lead them into it. The pizza and the orange were never the point.
The fraction was. Some readers find upaya freeing, because it explains why Buddhist teaching looks so different from place to place.
Others ask a sharper question, which the sutra takes up in the next chapter: if the teacher shapes the message, is that honest? A father with a burning house is coming to answer it.

how: In Mahayana Buddhism, upaya, skillful means, is the teaching that Buddhas and bodhisattvas adapt their words to their hearers; chapter two of the Lotus Sutra is the classic place it is taught, and Tiantai, Tendai and Nichiren teachers study it closely.

o: teaching in many ways, each fitted to the one who hears
a clever trick a teacher uses to win an argument
a set of rules for how a monk must sit and walk

games.q: many ways, one goal: tap the pairs.
p: asks the Buddha again and again

s: in chapter two the Buddha starts teaching the moment he is asked
he says the Buddha-knowledge is hard to understand and stops; Sariputra has to ask again, and a third time.
some of the assembly walk out as the Buddha begins, and he lets them go
the sutra says they thought they had already understood; he does not call them back.
skillful means says the Buddhas have many different goals for different people
the ways are many; the sutra says the purpose is one: to open the Buddha-knowledge to beings.

games.q: you are Sariputra. the Buddha says the knowledge of the Buddhas is too deep, and falls silent. what do you do?
o: ask him to go on, and keep asking
games.why: Sariputra asks, is refused, and asks again, and a third time. only then does the Buddha agree to teach.

practice: Choose something you know well: how to make rice, why you love a song, what your job is. Explain it silently the way you'd say it to a friend your age, then again as you would to a small child.
Notice what changed, the words, the pictures, the speed, and rest on the part that didn't move.

wordCard.voice: Upaya. Skillful means: teaching in many ways, each fitted to the one who hears, all pointing to one goal. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: means, method, way of approach; with kaushalya, skill, it names chapter two.

carryVoice: Your line: many ways, one goal. The orange, the pizza, the same fraction. That's today, done.
